title: Build a center you can keep
idea: Prepare the pawn break, then recapture toward the middle.

steps.prompt: You want a pawn on d4, but right now it would simply be lost. Which quiet pawn move makes d4 possible next turn?
steps.praise: c3 guards d4 and takes away the b4 and d4 squares from Black's pieces. Now the break is backed up.
steps.wrong: That doesn't prepare d4. Look for the pawn that would stand behind d4 and recapture there.

steps.prompt: Now strike. Hit the bishop and the e5 pawn at the same time.
steps.praise: d4 attacks two things at once and claims the center. Black must react rather than build.
steps.wrong: The preparation was for one specific push. Play the pawn into the center.

steps.prompt: Black took. How do you recapture so that you end up with two pawns abreast in the middle?
steps.praise: Pawns on d4 and e4 control c5, d5, e5 and f5. Pieces behind them now have room and targets.
steps.wrong: Recapture with a pawn. A piece on d4 would just be chased; a pawn there stays.

takeaway: Two center pawns side by side take squares away from every enemy piece. Prepare the break so you can recapture with a pawn.

title: New pieces first, king last
idea: Bring out a fresh piece each move and tuck the king away.

steps.prompt: Your knight is out. Which piece on the kingside still stands between your king and castling? Bring it to an active diagonal.
steps.praise: A new piece on an active square, and the path for the king is now clear.
steps.wrong: Moving a piece twice or pushing another pawn lets Black catch up. Bring out the bishop that is blocking your king.

steps.prompt: Everything is ready. Make the move that does two jobs at once: king to safety and rook toward the center.
steps.praise: Castled. The king is behind pawns and the rook can reach the open files first.
steps.wrong: Tempting, but your king is still on the file that opens first. Castle now while you can.

takeaway: In the opening, count pieces out, not pawn moves. Every extra tempo spent on one piece is a tempo your opponent spends on a new one.

title: When the guard has left
idea: With the f6 knight gone, the h7 pawn has lost its defender.

steps.prompt: Black's kingside knight has moved away from f6. What did that knight protect, and how can you exploit it right now, even at the cost of a bishop?
steps.praise: The Greek gift. You've given a bishop to drag the king out from behind its pawns.
steps.wrong: Look at the line from your d3 bishop to h7. Nothing guards that pawn except the king.

steps.prompt: The king stands on h7, exposed. Bring in a piece with check, and open the path for your queen.
steps.praise: The knight arrives with tempo, and it also clears the d1-h5 diagonal.
steps.wrong: You've spent a bishop, so every move must carry a threat. Use a check that also unblocks your queen.

steps.prompt: One more attacker. Where does the queen go to threaten mate on h7?
steps.praise: Queen and knight aim at h7, and Black has no time to bring the defenders home.
steps.wrong: Your queen has just been given a clear diagonal. Follow it to the h-file.

takeaway: Sacrifice when the defenders are away from the king. Before you give up material, count the attackers that can arrive with tempo.

title: Attack a chain at its base
idea: A pawn chain is only as strong as the pawn holding up the rest.

steps.prompt: White's chain runs d4 to e5. The e5 pawn depends on d4. Which pawn move hits that base at once?
steps.praise: c5 goes straight at the base of the chain. If d4 ever falls, e5 is left hanging.
steps.wrong: Attacking the head on e5 is hard work. Strike the pawn it stands on.

steps.prompt: White has shored up d4. Add a piece to the pressure.
steps.praise: Now two of your units aim at d4. White must keep defending it.
steps.wrong: Keep the target in mind. Which minor piece can reach a square that hits d4?

steps.prompt: Add a third attacker. The queen can do it, and watch b2 from the same square.
steps.praise: Pawn, knight and queen all hit d4, and b2 is under fire as well. White's pieces are tied to their pawns.
steps.wrong: Your queen has one square that attacks d4 and b2 together. Find it on the b-file.

takeaway: Don't charge the front of a pawn chain. Undermine the base, and every pawn above it starts to wobble.

title: Three against three, and a queen
idea: A sacrifice can turn equal pawns into an unstoppable one.

steps.prompt: The kings are far away. Three pawns face three, and pushing the wrong one blocks everything. Which pawn starts the breakthrough?
steps.praise: The middle pawn goes first. Either capture pulls a defender off its file.
steps.wrong: Pushing an outside pawn lets Black capture and hold the rest. Start from the middle.

steps.prompt: Black took with the a-pawn. Now the c-file: give up another pawn to deflect the last guard.
steps.praise: Now look at the a-file. Nothing stands between your pawn and the far edge.
steps.wrong: Capturing back just trades pawns off. You want Black's b7 pawn dragged away from a6.

steps.prompt: Run.
steps.praise: The black king is far outside the square of the pawn.
steps.wrong: The a-pawn is free. Push it.

steps.prompt: Keep going.
steps.praise: One square left.
steps.wrong: Don't stop. The a-pawn is one step from the seventh rank.

steps.prompt: Promote.
steps.praise: Two pawns given up, a queen gained.
steps.wrong: Promote the pawn to a queen.

takeaway: Pawns are currency. When the enemy king is far away, count whether giving up two brings one home.

title: A square no pawn can touch
idea: Without a c-pawn or e6 push, d5 is yours for good.

steps.prompt: Black's e-pawn has passed e6 and there is no c-pawn left. So no black pawn can ever attack one central square. Occupy it.
steps.praise: d5 is a hole in Black's position. Black had to give up a good knight to remove yours.
steps.wrong: Look at d5: which black pawns could ever chase a piece from there? Put a knight on it.

steps.prompt: Recapture in the way that gains space and hits the c6 knight.
steps.praise: Your pawn on d5 kicks the knight and cramps Black. The queenside and the e-file now open up for your rooks.
steps.wrong: A queen on d5 can be harassed. Take with the pawn, which also attacks c6.

takeaway: Before you push a pawn, ask which squares it can never guard again. Those holes are where enemy knights will live.

title: Rooks want open files
idea: One open file decides where both rooks belong.

steps.prompt: Only one file on the board has no pawns on it. Get there first.
steps.praise: The d-file belongs to you. Black has nothing to fight for it with right now.
steps.wrong: A rook behind its own pawn does nothing. Find the file with no pawns.

steps.prompt: An open file is a road. Where does it lead? Go in, right behind Black's pawns.
steps.praise: A rook on the seventh attacks pawns from behind and pins down the king.
steps.wrong: Don't wait on d1. Drive up to the seventh rank, where the pawns have no protection from behind.

steps.prompt: Black challenges. Bring the other rook onto the file so the seventh stays yours.
steps.praise: Doubled. If rooks are traded, you recapture and still own the seventh rank.
steps.wrong: Keep the file. Your other rook belongs directly behind the first.

takeaway: Find the open file, occupy it, invade along it, and back up the invader. The other rook is always part of the plan.

title: Trade your worst piece
idea: A bishop blocked by its own pawns should swap for a good one.

steps.prompt: Your c8 bishop is shut in by your own pawns on d5 and e6. White's light-squared bishop has no such trouble. Give yours a way out on the queenside. First, the pawn move.
steps.praise: b6 opens the a6-f1 diagonal for your bishop and keeps the knight free to guard a6.
steps.wrong: Your bishop can't get out past e6. It needs another exit, on the queenside.

steps.prompt: Now offer the trade.
steps.praise: The b8 knight guards a6, so if bishops come off you've swapped your worst piece for White's freest one.
steps.wrong: The diagonal you just opened runs straight at e2. Put the bishop on it.

takeaway: Bishops are judged by their own pawns. If yours are on its color, trade it, or put your pawns on the other color.

title: Go the long way round
idea: Two quiet moves move a knight from doing nothing to eyeing the king.

steps.prompt: Your d2 knight blocks the c1 bishop and has no future where it stands. It has one square to step back to, on the way to the kingside.
steps.praise: It looks like a retreat, but the bishop on c1 can breathe and the knight is on its way.
steps.wrong: Nothing is urgent here, so improve your worst piece. That's the d2 knight, and f1 is free.

steps.prompt: Finish the route. Where does this knight point at f5 and h5?
steps.praise: From g3 the knight eyes f5 and h5, right where Black's king lives.
steps.wrong: The knight is still only halfway. Continue toward the squares near Black's king.

takeaway: When there's nothing to attack, ask which piece is doing the least, and find it a better home, even if it takes a few moves.

title: What does your opponent want?
idea: Stop the threat before chasing your own plans.

steps.prompt: Before you attack anything, look at Black's rook. What would it do next if you passed? Solve that problem with one small pawn move.
steps.praise: Now your king has an escape square, so the back rank is no longer a death trap, and your rook is free to stay active.
steps.wrong: Black's rook reached your first rank, and your own pawns boxed in your king. Give the king a square.

takeaway: Every move, ask what your opponent would do if it were their turn again. Often the strongest move is a small one that says no.

title: Taking the opposition
idea: Kings facing each other: whoever must move gives way.

steps.prompt: Kings can't stand next to each other. Place yours directly facing Black's, two squares apart, so that Black must give way.
steps.praise: You took the opposition, and the black king had to step aside.
steps.wrong: Your king needs to lead the pawn. Pushing now lets Black's king block in front. Face the king first.

steps.prompt: Black stepped left. Go forward on the other side, so your king gets ahead of its pawn.
steps.praise: Outflanked. Your king now controls the squares the pawn must cross.
steps.wrong: Walk around the black king, not into it. The way past is on the kingside.

steps.prompt: With your king escorting, the pawn can advance.
steps.praise: The king clears the road and the pawn follows.
steps.wrong: Your king has done its work. Now move the pawn up.

steps.prompt: Keep it moving.
steps.praise: With the king in front and alongside its pawn, this ending is won.
steps.wrong: Advance the pawn again. It's guarded all the way.

takeaway: King and pawn endings turn on one square. Get your king in front of its pawn, and use the opposition to push the other king back.

title: Building a bridge
idea: The most useful rook ending: your king needs a roof to walk out under.

steps.prompt: Your king is stuck in front of your pawn, and it can't walk out while Black's rook checks it. First, drive the black king one file further away.
steps.praise: The black king is cut off from the queening corner.
steps.wrong: Black's king stands too close. Give a check on the d-file to push it away.

steps.prompt: Here's the famous quiet move. Put your rook on the fourth rank. It will block checks later.
steps.praise: This is the bridge. When checks come, your rook steps across and shields the king.
steps.wrong: Your rook needs to be ready to interpose, and only the fourth rank gives it that. Lift it to d4.

steps.prompt: Now the king comes out. Let the checks begin.
steps.praise: Checks will come from the c-file, your king walks toward the rook, and the rook blocks. The pawn queens.
steps.wrong: It's time. Step your king out diagonally to clear b8 for the pawn.

takeaway: Cut off the enemy king, lift your rook to the fourth rank, walk out, and block the last check. This is worth memorizing.

title: Before the file opens
idea: An uncastled king is a target as soon as the center opens.

steps.prompt: You're Black here. Both sides have developed. White's bishop eyes f7, and the center could crack at any moment. What's the sound move?
steps.praise: With the king safe and the rook on f8, the f7 square is guarded twice over, and you can now think about ...d6 and ...Be6.
steps.wrong: Your king sits on a file that can open with a single exchange. Get it out of there first.

takeaway: Castling isn't a formality. It takes one move and removes the easiest target in your position.
